verses.1: Al-Mizan treats the question as an aggrandizing introduction to the Day of Resurrection, called al-ghāshiyah because it may taghshá all people, cover them with terrors, or cover disbelievers’ faces with punishment.
verses.2: Al-Mizan says the people are humbled by covering sorrow and punishment, with humility attributed to their faces because it is most visible there. Nāṣibah derives from naṣab, synonymous with taʿab (exhaustion, fatigue). Its preferred contextual reading takes their labor as worldly striving whose works are annulled, leaving only exhaustion in the Hereafter (25:23). It records alternatives: they labor amid the fire’s punishments, or they labored in sin and become weary there.

verses.4: Al-Mizan says they enter a fire of the utmost heat.
verses.5: Al-Mizan says they drink from an āniyah spring, extremely hot and searing.
verses.6: Al-Mizan identifies ḍarīʿ as a dried thornbush, shabraq, known in Hejaz as an exceptionally unpleasant, coarse, and repellent plant which no animal eats. It suggests that the name may designate hell’s food only through resemblance in form and properties.

verses.8: Al-Mizan gives two derivations for nāʿimah: nuʿūmah (softness, fineness), figuratively describing joy visible on the face, or niʿmah (blessing, bounty), meaning endowed with blessings. It adds that, according to some, the missing conjunction separating this group from the humbled faces marks the wide gap between them.
verses.9: Al-Mizan reads saʿy as righteous striving in this world, for which the people will receive a good reward; the lām in li-saʿyihā is zāʾidah, added only for emphasis. Their lofty paradise is exalted in rank, honor, magnificence, and lushness, containing deathless life, painless pleasure, sorrowless joy, and whatever they wish. There they hear no idle, futile, or improper speech.

verses.12: Al-Mizan takes the flowing spring generically, while noting named springs such as Salsabīl (76:18). Raised surur indicate their occupants’ exalted rank; akwāb are drinking vessels without handle or spout; namāriq are cushions arranged like those in luxurious halls; and zarābī are elegant rugs spread for sitting. An editor’s note cautions that the purifying drink (76:21) is not identified as a spring.

verses.17: Al-Mizan presents reflection on the camel, sky, mountains, and earth as evidence of God’s direction of the world, His Lordship, the obligation of worshipping Him alone, and the coming reckoning. It points to the camel’s formation from dust and its many services to a Meccan Bedouin audience; the heavenly lights and life-sustaining atmosphere; mountains as stabilizers, water stores, and mineral reserves; and the leveled earth’s fitness for habitation and activity. These designed arrangements, it argues, establish the Enveloper as the day of retribution.

verses.21: Al-Mizan treats the fāʾ as drawing the conclusion that, since God alone is Lord and all face retribution, the Prophet must admonish them; his office is reminder, not coercion. Muṣayṭir means a guardian or supervisor and was originally musayṭir. It takes the exception as ending repeated admonition only after people reject the first reminder, leaving them to God’s greatest punishment in hell. It reports two alternatives—authority over persistent rejecters, or an unconnected exception—but calls its own reading more apparent.

verses.25: Al-Mizan says iyāb is synonymous with rujūʿ (return, referral). The fronted predicate emphasizes the return and preserves the surrounding rhyme, but does not express exclusivity, since no one claims that people return to anyone other than God.
verses.26: Al-Mizan says this verse matches the preceding one in meaning, structure, and construction.
